content.text: JavaScript's garbage collector frees memory that nothing can reach anymore. It can't free memory your code no longer needs but still references, and that's what a leak is in JavaScript: a listener left on
, a cache that only grows, a timer nobody clears. The fix is never "trust the GC"; it's cutting the reference.

Analysts keep a trading dashboard open all day, opening and closing chart panels. By the afternoon the tab is sluggish, and some days it crashes; a reload always "fixes" it. A heap snapshot tells the story: only one chart is on screen, yet hundreds of
objects are alive, each with its full array of price samples. Every chart that was ever closed is still in memory, and the code has a garbage collector the whole time.
The belief: JavaScript has a garbage collector, so memory leaks can't happen. Leaks are what you get in C, when you forget to call

There's real truth in it. You never free memory by hand in JavaScript, and the classic leak of manual memory management, an object nothing points to that nobody released, is exactly what a collector cleans up. Even reference cycles are fine: MDN notes that all modern engines use a

collector, which doesn't care whether unreachable objects point at each other. And most pages are short-lived: you navigate away, the whole heap goes, and a slow leak never gets the chance to show. The half-truth hides a second kind of leak that no collector can see.
The collector frees what's unreachable, not what's unused

MDN explains the trade-off. Knowing whether a piece of memory is still needed is undecidable in general, so collectors settle for an approximation: "no longer needed" becomes "unreachable". Starting from the roots (in JavaScript, the global object), the collector marks every object it can reach by following references, then frees the rest. If your code can still reach an object, even through a path you've forgotten about, it stays.
A JavaScript leak is a reference you forgot

blocks.title: Confirm the leak before you hunt for it

content.text: Open Chrome's Task Manager (Shift+Esc), enable the JavaScript memory column, and repeat the suspicious action, such as opening and closing a panel, a few dozen times. If memory keeps climbing, take a heap snapshot in the Memory panel and type
in the class filter to find elements still held by JavaScript.

blocks.title: WeakRef is not a cleanup strategy
